title: From bean definition to a bean you can use
summary: One method, doCreateBean, calls three others in order: instantiate, populate, initialise. Every lifecycle callback you have ever used hangs off one of those three.
entry: Put a breakpoint in AbstractAutowireCapableBeanFactory.doCreateBean, conditional on beanName.equals("yourBean"), and start the app. Everything below happens inside this one frame.

steps.notice: The singleton cache and the creation guard. Read this first: the three-map structure here (finished, early, factories) is the whole mechanism behind circular references.

The spine. createBeanInstance, then populateBean, then initializeBean. Everything else is a callback fired from one of those three, and reading them in order is the fastest way to understand the container.
Constructor resolution. Note that a single constructor needs no @Autowired, and that constructor arguments must be resolvable here, which is why a constructor cycle cannot work.

Called between instantiation and population: the half-built object is published so something else can reference it. This single line is why field injection tolerates a cycle and constructor injection does not.
Injection. It is not special-cased in the container; it is just InstantiationAwareBeanPostProcessor.postProcessProperties, and AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor is one such processor.

Where @Autowired fields and methods are actually set, using metadata collected earlier in postProcessMergedBeanDefinition. Being a PriorityOrdered processor, it runs before most other property callbacks.

Four steps in twenty lines: Aware callbacks, BeanPostProcessor before-init (this is where @PostConstruct runs), afterPropertiesSet and the custom init-method, then BeanPostProcessor after-init. That last step is where the auto-proxy creator swaps your object.
Shutdown in reverse: @PreDestroy, DisposableBean.destroy, then the custom destroy-method. Prototypes never get here, because the container stopped tracking them at handover.
